common_name: Little Woody Redbud (True Dwarf Vase-Shaped Redbud)

planting.note: Plant nursery stock in spring or early fall in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Little Woody is a true dwarf redbud selection, staying only 10-12 feet tall at maturity, well suited to small Gulf Coast landscapes where a standard-sized redbud would quickly outgrow the space.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Little Woody is a genuine dwarf redbud, selected in 2000 by North Carolina plantsman Paul Woody, reaching only 10-12 feet at maturity with a tidy, vase-shaped form rather than the larger spreading canopy of the straight species. In early spring, the bare branches are covered in the classic rosy-pink, pea-like redbud flowers before the heart-shaped leaves emerge, providing the same spectacular native spring display as a standard redbud but scaled for a small yard, courtyard, or foundation planting. Water deeply during the first two years to establish the root system, then supplement only during dry spells once established. Prune lightly just after flowering if any shaping is needed.

common_name: Jean's Appalachian Snow Dogwood (Anthracnose-Resistant White Flowering Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Jean's Appalachian Snow was bred at the University of Tennessee specifically for resistance to anthracnose and powdery mildew, two diseases that have devastated flowering dogwoods across much of the humid South.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Jean's Appalachian Snow is a University of Tennessee-bred flowering dogwood selected specifically for resistance to dogwood anthracnose and powdery mildew, two fungal diseases that have killed or badly disfigured flowering dogwoods across much of the humid South in recent decades, making disease-resistant selections like this one an increasingly important choice over older, more vulnerable cultivars. It produces the classic large, pure white bracts in early spring on a naturally graceful, horizontally branched small tree, followed by good fall color and red berries that feed birds. As an understory species, it performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade, mimicking its native woodland-edge habitat. Mulch heavily around the root zone to keep soil cool and moist through Gulf South summer heat.
sources: University of Tennessee — US Plant Patent PP13099

common_name: Enduring Summer Crapemyrtle (True Dwarf Reblooming Disease-Resistant Series)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Enduring Summer is a true dwarf crapemyrtle series, staying only 4-5 feet tall, bred with leaf-spot and powdery mildew resistance and a strong reblooming habit for a small Gulf Coast bed or container.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Enduring Summer is a true dwarf crapemyrtle series that stays a compact 4-5 feet tall, far smaller than the tree-form crapemyrtles that dominate most Gulf South landscapes, making it a good fit for small beds, foundation plantings, or large containers. It is bred with resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew and reblooms steadily through summer, especially if spent flower clusters are removed. Like other modern crapemyrtle introductions, it should be pruned lightly to remove only dead or crossing wood rather than subjected to the severe topping sometimes called 'crape murder,' which sacrifices natural form and delays bloom.

common_name: Delta Jazz Crapemyrtle (Dark Burgundy Foliage Hot-Pink Bloomer)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Delta Jazz is a Southern Living Plant Collection crapemyrtle bred for dark burgundy cupped foliage that provides strong color contrast against its hot-pink blooms through the heat of a Gulf South summer.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Delta Jazz stands out among crapemyrtles for its dark burgundy, distinctively cupped foliage that holds its rich color through summer heat, providing dramatic contrast against clusters of hot-pink blooms from summer into fall. It is heat-tolerant and generally resists deer browsing better than many other landscape shrubs, making it a durable choice for a Gulf South foundation planting or mixed border. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through the season. Prune lightly in late winter to remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches rather than heavily topping the plant, which sacrifices its natural form and delays bloom.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection — US Plant Patent PP21540

common_name: Center Stage Red Crapemyrtle (Black-Foliage Cerise-Red Compact Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Center Stage Red is a Proven Winners ColorChoice crapemyrtle bred by Spring Meadow Nursery for disease resistance and near-black foliage that dramatically sets off its cerise-red blooms, on a compact 10-12 foot form.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Center Stage Red bears near-black foliage that provides dramatic, season-long contrast to its clusters of vivid cerise-red flowers, standing out from the many crapemyrtle series bred primarily for flower color alone. Bred for good disease resistance, it holds its foliage well through a humid Gulf South summer, and its compact 10-12 foot mature size fits more readily into a residential landscape than older, larger crapemyrtle varieties. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued reblooming through the season, and prune only lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood, preserving the plant's natural vase-shaped form.
